entities.name: Andreas de Vega
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Andreas de Vega (died 1560) was a pivotal Spanish Franciscan theologian whose intellectual contributions profoundly shaped the Catholic Church's doctrinal responses during the Counter-Reformation. As a leading figure of the Observantine reform movement within the Franciscan Order, de Vega brought a rigorous scholastic approach to the theological debates of his era, particularly at the Council of Trent. His work cemented a significant portion of the Catholic position against Protestant reformers, underscoring the enduring power of scholasticism in the early modern intellectual landscape.

De Vega's most significant achievement was his active and influential participation in the Council of Trent (1545–1563), especially during its second period (1551–1552) under Pope Julius III. He served as a theological consultant, or *peritus*, contributing substantially to the formulation of decrees on justification and the sacraments, topics central to the theological schism with Protestantism. His detailed commentaries, later published as *Tridentini Decreta de Justificatione et Sacramentis* (1564), became a standard reference for explaining and defending the Council's teachings, offering a systematic exposition of Catholic doctrine that countered the interpretations of figures like Martin Luther and John Calvin.

The legacy of Andreas de Vega lies in his instrumental role in defining and solidifying Catholic orthodoxy in the face of widespread religious upheaval. His theological clarity and comprehensive defense of traditional doctrine provided intellectual ballast for the Counter-Reformation, influencing generations of Catholic theologians and shaping the curriculum of seminaries. His writings ensured that the Council of Trent's decrees were not merely pronouncements but were underpinned by a robust and accessible theological framework, thereby contributing to the Church's internal reform and external resilience.

His commentaries served as a definitive guide, influencing Catholic theology for centuries and directly countering Protestant interpretations.
